Lower Manhattan Is Thriving 25 Years After the Sept. 11 Attacks
 
Plus, a defunct mall in San Francisco is up for sale again
 
By Craig Karmin
 

This is an edition of the Real Estate newsletter, a weekly briefing of the biggest commercial deals, news, analysis and trends in office, multifamily, retail and other commercial sectors. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

In 2001, lower Manhattan was shattered. The Sept. 11 terrorist attacks killed close to 3,000 people and reduced the World Trade Center to rubble. Now, as the 25th anniversary of the event approaches, lower Manhattan is roaring back. Its population has roughly tripled over the past 25 years, and more than 230,000 people work there—nearly as many as before the attacks. Media and tech companies have moved in as banks and financial firms moved out. Peter Grant talks to the people who moved to the once blighted Financial District and examines why so many other American downtowns have failed to transform their business districts.

 

San Francisco has a 1.5-million-square-foot hole in its AI-fueled renaissance: the downtown site of what was its biggest mall. San Francisco Centre was a thriving retail destination, with a luxury day spa, nine-screen movie theater and department stores Nordstrom and Bloomingdale’s drawing huge crowds. But the mall got sucked into a downward spiral during the pandemic. Now, as Kate King reports, the mall is back on the market, with bids due Wednesday. Brokers expect it to sell for no more than $130 million—a shockingly meager sum compared with its $1.2 billion valuation a decade ago.

 
 
 

25 Years After the Sept. 11 Attacks, Lower Manhattan Is Thriving

 
 
CLARK HODGIN FOR WSJ
 

In 2001, lower Manhattan was shattered. The Sept. 11 terrorist attacks killed close to 3,000 people and reduced the World Trade Center to rubble. The Twin Towers’ shocking collapse inflicted such trauma that many wondered if the Financial District could ever recover.

 

Now, as the 25th anniversary of the event approaches, lower Manhattan is roaring back.

The amount of public and private money spent rebuilding the World Trade Center. That included about 10 million square feet of office space, nearly half a million square feet of retail, a transportation hub, the 9/11 Memorial and Museum and a performing arts center

Blackstone’s global head of real estate is leaving the firm, according to people familiar with the matter, the latest in a recent wave of departures from one of the world’s largest and most successful commercial-property investors.

 
 
 

Data Points

 

• 123,000: The amount, in square feet, of new luxury retail space that opened in the first half of 2026, a 46% year-over-year decline, according to JLL. After several years of rapid expansion in secondary markets, luxury executives are now slowing store-count growth but investing heavily in new flagship locations.

 

• $4.6 billion: Sale leaseback volume in the second quarter, bringing these transactions to their strongest half-year start since 2022, according to SLB Capital Advisors. Large portfolio sales drove the dollar volume, with the industrial sector comprising the highest number of transactions.
